title: Competency demonstration and patient safety
audience: Cleaners and cleaning supervisors who will carry out external cleaning of authorised medical equipment in a healthcare facility, in any Australian state or territory. This course covers external cleaning only.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4 (November 2021), Core Module (no page date shown), which has only been partly confirmed; Aged Care Quality Standards, Action 3.17 (guidance resource): reprocessing reusable equipment and devices ('Last updated' label, no date), which has only been partly confirmed.
learningOutcomes: Explain how screening, classification, instructions, exposure controls, surface work, transport and handoff work together in one task.
Demonstrate stop-work and escalation decisions in a supervised simulation with approved, restricted and unknown equipment.
Describe the difference between written knowledge and observed practical competence, and why only the second supports a work decision.
Explain how patient safety depends on the cleaner stopping at the boundary of their authority.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson: external cleaning only
instruction.body: This lesson covers external cleaning only. It brings together the earlier lessons into one supervised demonstration. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course. They are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility's written procedure. A demonstration in this course does not authorise any reprocessing, sterilisation or device disinfection, and it does not show competence for those tasks.

instruction.heading: What a competent external clean looks like
instruction.body: Competence in this course is the ability to complete one task safely from start to finish. Before touching an item, the cleaner confirms the written authority, the asset identity and the classification record, and reads the manufacturer instruction and product label. The cleaner selects protective equipment from the data sheet, performs hand hygiene, and cleans only the surfaces the instruction permits, using the approved method and contact condition. The cleaner keeps clean and used items apart, completes the handoff, and records the outcome honestly. At any point, a cleaner who cannot meet a requirement stops and escalates. Stopping is part of competent work, not a failure of it.

instruction.heading: The stop-work decision
instruction.body: The most important decision in this course is the stop. Stop when the authority is unclear, when the item is critical, semicritical or unknown, when the instruction is missing or conflicts, when the protection is not available, when the contact condition cannot be met, when the item is damaged or powered in an unexpected way, and when the request goes beyond your list. Stopping does not mean doing nothing. Make the area safe, leave the item as found, tell the responsible person, and record the decision. Patient safety depends on this decision being made consistently, including when someone is pressing you to finish quickly.

instruction.heading: Knowledge is not practical competence
instruction.body: Passing a written check shows that you can recall rules. It does not show that you can perform a task on a real item, in a real room, with a real trolley and a real colleague asking you for a shortcut. Practical competence is observed by a supervisor against defined criteria, on the facility's equipment, and recorded separately. A completed course, a knowledge check, or a certificate of attendance does not by itself authorise you to carry out any task. The facility decides when a person is competent for a specific task and records that decision.

instruction.heading: Worked simulation: the multi-device room
instruction.body: In a simulated treatment room you find four items: an approved trolley of external cleaning products, a restricted reusable instrument that is not on your list, a damaged powered unit with a split cable, and an unidentified device with no label. The competent response is to clean the approved trolley's surfaces only as the instructions allow, leave the restricted instrument and the unidentified device exactly where they are, leave the damaged powered unit untouched, make the room safe, and escalate all three. Record each item separately, the decision for each, and the person notified. The task is not complete while any item remains unresolved.

procedure: Confirm written authority for each item and check the facility classification record before any contact.
Read the manufacturer instruction and the product label, and select the approved product and contact condition.
Select and check protective equipment, and perform hand hygiene before starting.
Clean only the authorised surfaces, keeping keep-dry areas dry and maintaining the required contact condition.
Stop and escalate immediately on any restricted, unknown, damaged or unclear item, and leave it as found.
Keep clean and used items separate, and complete the handoff to the receiving person.
Record the outcome, including any stopped item, the decision made and the person notified, and sign only for what you observed.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor is observing your external clean of a bed-side table. As you finish, the supervisor asks you to also wipe a reusable instrument on the same table to save a return visit.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you respond, and what does the supervisor's observation show?
workedExamples.reasoning: Decline the instrument. It is not on your authorised list, and wiping it would be an unauthorised reprocessing step. Explain the reason, leave the instrument, and tell the supervisor it needs the reprocessing team. The observation shows that the cleaner stopped at the authority boundary. This response is part of the competency, not a deviation from it.

workedExamples.situation: A trainee cleaner completes the external clean of an authorised monitor, but does not record the contact condition because the wipe dried early.
workedExamples.reasoning: The supervisor records the task as incomplete and notes that the trainee did not record the unmet condition. The trainee is asked to correct the record and to explain the next step. The demonstration is not passed on that criterion until the record is accurate.

commonErrors.error: Treating a course completion or knowledge check as permission to carry out any task.
commonErrors.prevention: Only the facility's practical assessment and its written authorisation allow a task.

commonErrors.error: Completing the external clean of an approved item and then also cleaning a restricted item on the same surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Assess each item separately. Leave the restricted item and escalate.

commonErrors.error: Treating a stop as a failure and then rushing the remaining steps to recover.
commonErrors.prevention: A stop is a correct decision. Record it and escalate. Do not rush to compensate.

commonErrors.error: Signing for a practical criterion that the supervisor did not observe.
commonErrors.prevention: Sign only for what was observed. Unobserved criteria remain open.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This course covers external cleaning only. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside the course and are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the facility procedure.

Licence notice: A completed course, knowledge check or demonstration does not grant any licence, certificate, registration or authority to do regulated work, including reprocessing, electrical work or waste transport. The facility decides competence for specific tasks.

The NDIS Practice Standards, Version 4 of November 2021, Core Module, require each worker to be trained in standard precautions and in PPE use, with refresher training. Where the facility is an NDIS provider, these requirements apply to the facility.
The Aged Care Quality Standards Action 3.17 guidance resource (no date shown) refers to workforce training for reprocessing.

qualityStandard: In a supervised simulation, the learner completes a full external clean on an approved item, with each step observed against the criteria.
The learner stops and escalates a restricted, unknown and damaged item in the same simulation, and records each decision separately.
The learner states, without prompting, the difference between written knowledge and observed practical competence.
The supervisor signs only for criteria observed, and records any criterion not met with the reason.
documentationEvidence: Supervisor observation sheet against each practical criterion, signed by the observer
Work record for the approved item, with the contact condition and product recorded
Stop and escalation records for each restricted, unknown or damaged item
summary: A competent external clean is one task done safely from confirmed authority to honest record.
Stopping at the boundary of your authority is a core competence, and it protects the patient.
Knowledge checks and course completion do not authorise a task. Practical competence is observed and recorded by the facility.
This course does not show competence in reprocessing, sterilisation or device disinfection.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement best describes practical competence in this course?
options: A cleaner who passes the knowledge check is competent for all tasks at the facility and on every device
Practical competence is observed by a supervisor against defined criteria and recorded by the facility.
A course certificate is enough to start any task on any equipment in the facility today

knowledgeChecks.question: In a room with an approved item, a restricted instrument and an unidentified device, what is the correct action?
options: Clean all three items with the approved product to finish the room.
Move the restricted instrument and the unidentified device to clean stock to be safe.
Clean the approved item within its instruction, leave the other two as found, and escalate them.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is stopping at the boundary of authority part of competent work?
options: Because it prevents unauthorised or unsafe work, which protects the patient and the worker.
Because it lets the cleaner finish the round faster and the job is completed sooner for the client
Because stopping always avoids the need for a record of the work that was done on the day
